pages.title: What this unit is about
pages.body:
> 🧩 **Strand 4 — Computational Thinking**
Sub-strand 4: Artificial Intelligence

Before machine learning became popular, AI researchers built expert systems that capture human expertise as rules. In this unit you will query an expert system with IF–THEN rules and train your own machine learning model.

pages.title: Expert Systems, Telemedicine and Teachable Machine
pages.body:
Curriculum indicator B9.4.4.1.1
> 🎯 **Learning objectives** By the end of this lesson you should be able to:
- describe expert systems;
- illustrate the IF–THEN control structure for querying an expert system;
- use Google’s Teachable Machine to understand machine learning.
An **expert system** (knowledge-based system) is a computer program that imitates the decision-making of a **human expert** in a specific field, such as medicine, agriculture or car repair. It is called **classical AI** because it uses explicit **rules** written by humans rather than learning from data. A famous early example is **MYCIN** (Stanford University, 1970s), which suggested treatments for blood infections.
[[fig:c9-f18|Figure 17: The parts of an expert system]]
| **Component** | **Function** |
|---|---|
| Knowledge base | Stores facts and **IF–THEN rules** obtained from experts |
| Inference engine | The “reasoning” part: matches the user’s facts with the rules to reach conclusions |
| User interface | Asks the user questions and shows the answers |
| Explanation facility | Explains how a conclusion was reached |

pages.title: Querying an expert system with IF–THEN rules
pages.body:
## Querying an expert system with IF–THEN rules
> ✏️ **Worked example — A simple health-advice expert system**
RULE 1: IF fever = yes AND chills = yes AND headache = yes THEN advise "Possible malaria: visit a health centre for a test"
RULE 2: IF fever = yes AND cough = yes AND difficulty breathing = yes THEN advise "Seek medical care urgently"
RULE 3: IF rash = yes AND itching = yes AND fever = no THEN advise "Possible allergy: see a pharmacist or nurse"
RULE 4: IF none of the rules apply THEN advise "Monitor symptoms; consult a health worker if they persist"
**Query:** The user answers fever: yes, chills: yes, headache: yes. The inference engine finds that Rule 1 matches and outputs its advice, explaining that it used Rule 1.
This is a learning example only; real medical decisions must be made by qualified health professionals.
## Telemedicine
**Telemedicine** is the delivery of health care at a distance using ICT: phone and video consultations, sending photos or test results to specialists, and knowledge-based systems that guide health workers in remote areas. In a telemedicine system, a community health nurse can **input a request** (symptoms, readings), and the system or a remote doctor returns **advice or a referral**, which saves travel time and lives.
## Machine learning with Google’s Teachable Machine
Unlike an expert system, a **machine learning** system is not given rules; it **learns from examples**. Google’s free **Teachable Machine** website (teachablemachine.withgoogle.com) lets you train a model in your browser to recognise images, sounds or poses.

pages.title: Querying an expert system with IF–THEN rules (continued)
pages.body:
[[fig:c9-f19|Figure 18: Training a model with Teachable Machine]]
> 🪜 **Step by step — Training an image model**
1. Open teachablemachine.withgoogle.com and click **Get Started › Image Project › Standard image model**.
2. Rename **Class 1** to Pen and **Class 2** to Book. Click **Webcam** and hold each object in front of the camera to record about 50–100 example images per class (vary angles and lighting).
3. Click **Train Model** and wait; do not switch browser tabs.
4. In **Preview**, show a pen or a book to the webcam and read the **confidence** percentages.
5. Test with a new object (e.g. a ruler). What does the model predict? Why?
6. Add a third class, add more examples, retrain and compare the accuracy.
> 💡 **Think About It How Data Is Collected And Used** The model is only as good as its **training data**: too few, unclear or one-sided examples give wrong predictions (**bias**). Teachable Machine trains in your browser, but when apps collect photos, voices or faces, ask: Who keeps the data? For what purpose? Did people give permission? Object-recognition apps such as **Google Lens** work the same way, using models trained on millions of images.
| **Expert system (classical AI)** | **Machine learning** |
|---|---|
| Rules written by human experts | Patterns learnt from example data |
| Easy to explain its reasoning | Often hard to explain (“black box”) |
| Hard to update when knowledge changes | Improves with more data |
| Works with little data | Needs lots of data and computing power |

pages.body:
> ✏️ **Review exercises** — answer these in your exercise book or on the computer, then check with your teacher.
## Short answer questions
1. Describe the **four** components of an expert system.
2. Write **three** IF–THEN rules for an expert system that advises farmers on when to plant maize.
3. Explain how telemedicine benefits rural communities.
4. Compare expert systems with machine learning.
